claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing has not yet been widely applied to single-celled organisms.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing is revolutionising our understanding of seemingly homogeneous cell populations but has not yet been widely applied to single-celled organisms.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract about the state of the field at the time of writing.

claim: Transcriptional variation in unicellular malaria parasites from the Plasmodium genus is associated with critical phenotypes including red blood cell invasion and immune evasion.
source: Transcriptional variation in unicellular malaria parasites from the Plasmodium genus is associated with critical phenotypes including red blood cell invasion and immune evasion, yet transcriptional variation at an individual parasite level has not been examined in depth.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about Plasmodium biology.

claim: Transcriptional variation at an individual parasite level has not been examined in depth.
source: Transcriptional variation in unicellular malaria parasites from the Plasmodium genus is associated with critical phenotypes including red blood cell invasion and immune evasion, yet transcriptional variation at an individual parasite level has not been examined in depth.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The study adapted a single-cell RNA-sequencing protocol to analyze more than 500 individual parasites of both rodent and human malaria comprising asexual and sexual life-cycle stages.
source: Here, we describe the adaptation of a single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) protocol to deconvolute transcriptional variation for more than 500 individual parasites of both rodent and human malaria comprising asexual and sexual life-cycle stages.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The study uncovered previously hidden discrete transcriptional signatures during the pathogenic part of the life cycle.
source: We uncover previously hidden discrete transcriptional signatures during the pathogenic part of the life cycle, suggesting that expression over development is not as continuous as commonly thought.
evidence: This is a major finding from the study's analysis of single-cell data.

claim: Expression over development is not as continuous as commonly thought.
source: We uncover previously hidden discrete transcriptional signatures during the pathogenic part of the life cycle, suggesting that expression over development is not as continuous as commonly thought.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the discrete transcriptional signatures observed.

claim: The study found novel, sex-specific roles for differential expression of contingency gene families in transmission stages.
source: In transmission stages, we find novel, sex-specific roles for differential expression of contingency gene families that are usually associated with immune evasion and pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of sexual stage parasites.

claim: Contingency gene families are usually associated with immune evasion and pathogenesis.
source: In transmission stages, we find novel, sex-specific roles for differential expression of contingency gene families that are usually associated with immune evasion and pathogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about contingency gene families.

claim: Malaria is caused by unicellular eukaryotic parasites from the Plasmodium genus.
source: Malaria is caused by unicellular eukaryotic parasites from the Plasmodium genus.
evidence: This is basic established knowledge about malaria.

claim: Asexual intra-erythrocytic replication of parasites is solely responsible for pathogenesis in the blood of infected patients.
source: In the blood of infected patients, asexual intra-erythrocytic replication of parasites is solely responsible for pathogenesis, whilst sexual stages, termed gametocytes, are the only stage capable of transmission to the next host via the mosquito vector.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria parasite biology.

claim: Sexual stages, termed gametocytes, are the only stage capable of transmission to the next host via the mosquito vector.
source: In the blood of infected patients, asexual intra-erythrocytic replication of parasites is solely responsible for pathogenesis, whilst sexual stages, termed gametocytes, are the only stage capable of transmission to the next host via the mosquito vector.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria parasite transmission.

claim: Distinct life stages have been extensively investigated using transcriptomic approaches at a population level.
source: These distinct life stages have been extensively investigated using transcriptomic approaches (Otto et al., 2010; Bozdech et al., 2003a; López-Barragán et al., 2011; Llinás et al., 2006; Hall et al., 2005; Lasonder et al., 2016; Otto et al., 2014), but this has been largely at a population level.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Little is known about how individual cells vary within stages.
source: Little is known about how individual cells vary within stages.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq produces transcriptomic profiles for multiple individual cells.
source: Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) produces transcriptomic profiles for multiple individual cells.
evidence: This is a definition of the scRNA-seq technique.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq has allowed the decomposition of cell populations.
source: This has allowed the decomposition of cell populations (Haber et al., 2017), uncovered previously unknown cell types (Grün et al., 2015) and enhanced our understanding of developmental pathways (Mohammed et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haber et al., 2017.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq has uncovered previously unknown cell types.
source: This has allowed the decomposition of cell populations (Haber et al., 2017), uncovered previously unknown cell types (Grün et al., 2015) and enhanced our understanding of developmental pathways (Mohammed et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grün et al., 2015.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq has enhanced our understanding of developmental pathways.
source: This has allowed the decomposition of cell populations (Haber et al., 2017), uncovered previously unknown cell types (Grün et al., 2015) and enhanced our understanding of developmental pathways (Mohammed et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mohammed et al., 2017.

claim: Several scRNA-seq methods with different attributes have been described.
source: Several scRNA-seq methods with different attributes have now been described (Ziegenhain et al., 2017), with some providing depth – a good representation of full length transcripts (Picelli et al., 2013) from tens or hundreds of cells – and others providing breadth, with poorer representation of transcriptomes but from a much greater number of cells (Macosko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies describing different methods.

claim: Some scRNA-seq methods provide depth with good representation of full length transcripts from tens or hundreds of cells.
source: Several scRNA-seq methods with different attributes have now been described (Ziegenhain et al., 2017), with some providing depth – a good representation of full length transcripts (Picelli et al., 2013) from tens or hundreds of cells – and others providing breadth, with poorer representation of transcriptomes but from a much greater number of cells (Macosko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Picelli et al., 2013.

claim: Some scRNA-seq methods provide breadth with poorer representation of transcriptomes but from a much greater number of cells.
source: Several scRNA-seq methods with different attributes have now been described (Ziegenhain et al., 2017), with some providing depth – a good representation of full length transcripts (Picelli et al., 2013) from tens or hundreds of cells – and others providing breadth, with poorer representation of transcriptomes but from a much greater number of cells (Macosko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Macosko et al., 2015.

claim: A recent study demonstrated the use of Drop-seq to identify a signature of sexual commitment in Plasmodium.
source: A recent study (Poran et al., 2017) demonstrated the use of a high-throughput, low-coverage scRNA-seq technique (Drop-seq [Macosko et al., 2015]) to identify a signature of sexual commitment in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Poran et al., 2017.

claim: The study uses a lower throughput but higher coverage approach compared to Drop-seq.
source: Here, we use a lower throughput (fewer cells), but higher coverage (both more genes detected and more of each gene's length detected via full-length transcript sequencing) approach to examine transcriptional dynamics of the parasite during the blood stages in both the most popular rodent model parasite (P. berghei) and the most deadly human malaria parasite (P. falciparum).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the current study.

claim: The study examined transcriptional dynamics during blood stages in both P. berghei and P. falciparum.
source: Here, we use a lower throughput (fewer cells), but higher coverage (both more genes detected and more of each gene's length detected via full-length transcript sequencing) approach to examine transcriptional dynamics of the parasite during the blood stages in both the most popular rodent model parasite (P. berghei) and the most deadly human malaria parasite (P. falciparum).
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: The method is highly effective at capturing transcriptional variation associated with different parasite stages and cell cycle states.
source: We show that this method is highly effective at capturing transcriptional variation associated with different parasite stages and cell cycle states, and we also uncover previously unknown aspects of the parasite's progression through its asexual cycle and in its sexual stages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's results.

claim: The study uncovered previously unknown aspects of the parasite's progression through its asexual cycle and in its sexual stages.
source: We show that this method is highly effective at capturing transcriptional variation associated with different parasite stages and cell cycle states, and we also uncover previously unknown aspects of the parasite's progression through its asexual cycle and in its sexual stages.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The greatest coverage of genes in mammalian cells using scRNA-seq has been achieved with the Smart-Seq2 protocol.
source: The greatest coverage of genes in mammalian cells using scRNA-seq has been achieved with the Smart-Seq2 protocol (Picelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Picelli et al., 2013.

claim: Smart-Seq2 is a plate-based approach that tends to result in detection of more transcripts from more genes than other approaches.
source: This plate-based approach tends to result in detection of more transcripts from more genes than other approaches (Svensson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Svensson et al., 2017.

claim: Smart-Seq2 is a full-length transcript method, providing information about transcript structure.
source: Furthermore, it is a full-length transcript method, providing information about transcript structure, allowing deconvolution of splicing variants and inference about the strand of origin (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2015.

claim: The standard Smart-seq2 protocol was initially trialled with 30 PCR cycles instead of 18 to account for the relatively low RNA content of protozoan cells.
source: Initially, we trialled the standard version of the Smart-seq2 protocol (Picelli et al., 2013) on sorted, Plasmodium falciparum-infected single red blood cells (Figure 1A), adjusting only the number of PCR cycles (30 rather than 18) to account for the relatively low RNA content of protozoan cells.
evidence: This describes the initial experimental approach.

claim: On average, only 10% of reads mapped to genes in the parasite genome using the standard Smart-seq2 protocol.
source: However, on average, only 10% of reads mapped to genes in the parasite genome and more than half of these mapped to rRNA genes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the initial trial shown in Figure 1B.

claim: More than half of the reads that mapped to genes in the parasite genome mapped to rRNA genes using the standard Smart-seq2 protocol.
source: However, on average, only 10% of reads mapped to genes in the parasite genome and more than half of these mapped to rRNA genes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the initial trial shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A longer, unanchored oligo(dT) primer (T30) significantly improved yield.
source: A longer, unanchored oligo(dT) primer (T30) significantly improved yield and SuperScript II and SMARTScribe were the highest yielding reverse transcriptases (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from optimization experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SuperScript II and SMARTScribe were the highest yielding reverse transcriptases.
source: A longer, unanchored oligo(dT) primer (T30) significantly improved yield and SuperScript II and SMARTScribe were the highest yielding reverse transcriptases (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from optimization experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Significantly more genes were detected with dramatically reduced rRNA contamination using the SMARTScribe enzyme.
source: Significantly more genes were detected, with dramatically reduced rRNA contamination, using the SMARTScribe enzyme (Figure 1D; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from optimization experiments shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: No evidence for doublet events was found in the dual sort experiment.
source: No evidence for doublet events was found (Figure 2A) and, for each cell, the vast majority of reads (98.1% for P.berghei, 99.4% for P. falciparum) mapped uniquely to the genome of the expected species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the dual sort experiment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For each cell in the dual sort experiment, the vast majority of reads (98.1% for P.berghei, 99.4% for P. falciparum) mapped uniquely to the genome of the expected species.
source: No evidence for doublet events was found (Figure 2A) and, for each cell, the vast majority of reads (98.1% for P.berghei, 99.4% for P. falciparum) mapped uniquely to the genome of the expected species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the dual sort experiment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only 15 of 3566 transcripts detected in P. berghei cells were from P. falciparum.
source: Only 15 of 3566 transcripts detected in P. berghei cells were from P. falciparum, and none of these were differentially expressed, suggesting they will not affect our downstream analysis.
evidence: This is a result from the contamination analysis.

claim: None of the P. falciparum transcripts detected in P. berghei cells were differentially expressed.
source: Only 15 of 3566 transcripts detected in P. berghei cells were from P. falciparum, and none of these were differentially expressed, suggesting they will not affect our downstream analysis.
evidence: This is a result from the contamination analysis.

claim: The study generated 188 single-cell transcriptomes of mixed asexual and sexual blood-stage parasites of P. berghei.
source: Having established the reliability of the protocol, we generated 188 single-cell transcriptomes of mixed asexual and sexual (gametocyte) blood-stage parasites of the rodent malaria model P. berghei.
evidence: This describes the data generated in the study.

claim: After filtering, 144 high-quality transcriptomes remained from the P. berghei dataset.
source: After filtering to remove transcriptomes with fewer than 25,000 total reads and fewer than 1000 detected genes (with at least one read), 144 high-quality transcriptomes remained.
evidence: This describes the data filtering process.

claim: The study detected expression of 4579 genes in the P. berghei dataset, over 90% of genes in the P. berghei genome.
source: In total, we detected expression of 4579 genes: over 90% of genes in the P. berghei genome.
evidence: This is a result from the P. berghei dataset analysis.

claim: From each P. berghei cell, on average 1981 genes (~33%) were identified, similar to the proportion of transcriptomes detected in mammalian single-cell experiments.
source: From each cell, we identified expression from, on average, 1981 genes (~33%), similar to the proportion of transcriptomes detected in mammalian single-cell experiments (Treutlein et al., 2014) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the P. berghei dataset analysis, compared to mammalian studies.

claim: The study generated 191 high-quality single-cell transcriptomes for P. falciparum sexual stages, with an average 2090 genes detected.
source: This resulted in 191 high-quality single-cell transcriptomes (of 237 total) for sexual stages, with an average 2090 genes detected, and 161 high-quality single-cell transcriptomes (of 174 total) for asexual stages, with an average 1712 genes detected (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the P. falciparum dataset.

claim: The study generated 161 high-quality single-cell transcriptomes for P. falciparum asexual stages, with an average 1712 genes detected.
source: This resulted in 191 high-quality single-cell transcriptomes (of 237 total) for sexual stages, with an average 2090 genes detected, and 161 high-quality single-cell transcriptomes (of 174 total) for asexual stages, with an average 1712 genes detected (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the P. falciparum dataset.

claim: Neither GC content nor gene length had an impact on transcript detection.
source: In fact, neither GC content (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) nor gene length (Figure 2C) had an impact on transcript detection.
evidence: This is a result from the bias analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A slight 5' bias was detected in the data.
source: Many RNA-seq approaches display a signal bias towards the 5' or 3' end of transcripts and in our data, a slight 5' bias was detected that might also reflect binding of oligo(dT) to internal polyA-rich regions of transcripts (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from the bias analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Using PCA, k-means clustering, and comparison to bulk transcriptome datasets, each P. berghei cell was classified as male, female, or asexual.
source: Using a combination of Principal Components Analysis (PCA), k-means clustering using SC3 (Kiselev, 2016), and comparison to bulk transcriptome datasets (Otto et al., 2014; Hoo et al., 2016), we classified each cell as male, female, or asexual (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the classification method used.

claim: The accuracy of the classification was strongly supported by established stage-specific markers.
source: The accuracy of our classification was strongly supported by established stage-specific markers (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a validation of the classification method shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The confirmed absence of contaminating parasites of other life-cycle stages enabled determination of a new, longer list of stage-specific markers.
source: Moreover, the confirmed absence of contaminating parasites of other life-cycle stages enabled us to determine a new, longer list of stage-specific markers (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the classification analysis.

claim: Bulk RNA-seq studies have consistently revealed a continuous cascade of transcription initiation along the asexual cycle.
source: Bulk RNA-seq studies monitoring transcriptional patterns along the complete asexual cycle of both human and rodent malaria parasite species have consistently revealed a continuous cascade of transcription initiation (Hoo et al., 2016; Bozdech et al., 2003b) similar to that seen in other eukaryotes (Spellman et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings from bulk RNA-seq studies, supported by citations.

claim: Pseudotime analysis orders cells into developmental trajectories by identifying cells with transcriptomes that are most similar to each other.
source: Pseudotime analysis orders cells into developmental trajectories by identifying cells with transcriptomes that are most similar to each other and placing those closest to each other in order.
evidence: This is a description of the pseudotime analysis method.

claim: The cell orderings determined by pseudotime analysis were highly concordant with previously published transcriptional studies of the developmental time course.
source: The cell orderings determined by pseudotime analysis were highly concordant with previously published transcriptional studies of the developmental time course (Otto et al., 2010; López-Barragán et al., 2011; Otto et al., 2014; Hoo et al., 2016)(Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a result from the pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Single Plasmodium cells from an unsynchronised pool can be ordered by their transcriptional signatures to accurately derive a transcriptional map of development in the late asexual cycle.
source: This demonstrates that single Plasmodium cells from an unsynchronised pool can be ordered by their transcriptional signatures to accurately derive a transcriptional map of development in the late asexual cycle (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pseudotime analysis results shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In stark contrast to the smooth transitions observed in bulk time course experiments, abrupt changes in gene expression were observed during the cell cycle of both P. berghei and P. falciparum.
source: In stark contrast to the smooth transitions observed previously in bulk time course experiments (Bozdech et al., 2003a; Hoo et al., 2016), we observed abrupt changes in gene expression during the cell cycle of both P. berghei and P. falciparum (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a major finding from the pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single-cell data clearly revealed an abrupt transition in expression for genes that show a continuous cascade in bulk RNA-seq data.
source: Whereas a continuous cascade of transcription initiation along the asexual cycle can be seen in bulk RNA-seq data, single-cell data clearly revealed an abrupt transition in expression for the same genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from comparing bulk and single-cell data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Step-wise progression in the cycle represents a departure from the common view and suggests a previously hidden transcriptional pattern, conserved across Plasmodium parasites.
source: Step-wise progression in the cycle represents a departure from the common view and suggests a previously hidden transcriptional pattern, conserved across Plasmodium parasites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the abrupt transcriptional changes observed.

claim: Averaging across slightly asynchronous life cycle stages in bulk RNA-seq studies has previously masked the true nature of transitions along the asexual cell cycle.
source: We suspect that averaging across slightly asynchronous life cycle stages in bulk RNA-seq studies has previously masked the true nature of transitions along the asexual cell cycle.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the difference between bulk and single-cell results.

claim: Individual parasites do not proceed along an incremental path of transcriptional change, but instead generally appear to undergo transcriptional shifts, turning on or shutting down expression of a whole repertoire of genes simultaneously.
source: Individual parasites do not proceed along an incremental path of transcriptional change, but instead generally appear to undergo transcriptional shifts, turning on or shutting down expression of a whole repertoire of genes simultaneously.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the abrupt transcriptional changes observed.

claim: A k-means analysis in pseudotime identified three clusters of genes for each species.
source: A k-means analysis in pseudotime identified three clusters of genes (Trapnell et al., 2014) for each species (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cluster 1 in P. berghei was enriched for protein dynamics and energy metabolism including many ribosomal subunits, proteasome subunits and ATPases.
source: Cluster 1 in P. berghei (equivalent to cluster 2 in P. falciparum; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) was enriched for protein dynamics and energy metabolism including many ribosomal subunits, proteasome subunits and ATPases (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cluster 2 in P. berghei was associated with the rhoptry secretory organelle.
source: Cluster 2 in P. berghei (equivalent to cluster 3 in P. falciparum) was associated with the rhoptry secretory organelle, including ron2, ron4, ron5, ron12, rop14, rap1 and rap2/3.
evidence: This is a result from the functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Cluster 3 in P. berghei was enriched for the microneme secretory organelle and the inner membrane complex.
source: Cluster 3 in P. berghei was enriched for the microneme secretory organelle and the inner membrane complex, including sub2, ama1, ripr, imc1c, imc1e, imc1f, imc1g, imc1m and isp3.
evidence: This is a result from the functional enrichment analysis.

claim: These clusters may represent discrete transcriptional modules that underlie parasitic cell cycle checkpoints during the transition from a metabolically active, fast growing trophozoite to a budding multinucleated schizont.
source: These clusters may represent discrete transcriptional modules that underlie parasitic cell cycle checkpoints during the transition from a metabolically active, fast growing trophozoite to a budding multinucleated schizont.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the biological significance of the clusters.

claim: Two essential ApiAP2 transcription factors were associated with equivalent gene expression clusters in both species.
source: We note that two essential ApiAP2 transcription factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) were associated with equivalent gene expression clusters in both species: PBANKA_1453700 (PF3D7_1239200) with the early cluster (1) and PBANKA_0939100 (PF3D7_1107800) with the late cluster (2), implicating them as potential regulators of these modules.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The point at which Plasmodium parasites are within their cell cycle dominates the transcriptional variation observed within a genetically clonal population.
source: Like many other cell types (Spellman et al., 1998; Kowalczyk et al., 2015), the point at which Plasmodium parasites are within their cell cycle dominates the transcriptional variation observed within a genetically clonal population.
evidence: This is a statement about the major source of variation, supported by citations to other cell types.

claim: There are genes that vary independently of the cell cycle including clonally variant gene families.
source: However, there are also genes that vary independently of the cell cycle including clonally variant gene families, which are found largely in the subtelomeric regions of the genome (Rovira-Graells et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about cell-cycle-independent variation, supported by a citation.

claim: A unique chromatin environment is thought to allow switching between expression of different members of gene families.
source: A unique chromatin environment is thought to allow switching between expression of different members of gene families and this mechanism allows parasite populations to adapt to the host immune system (var genes) (Scherf et al., 2008), establish chronic infection (pir genes) (Scherf et al., 2008) and vary red blood cell invasion pathways (p235) (Preiser et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of gene family switching, supported by citations.

claim: 56 genes in P. falciparum asexual cells showed residual variation after adjusting for cell cycle variation.
source: After adjusting for these, we identified 56 genes in P. falciparum asexual cells that showed residual variation (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the scLVM analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Unlike clonally variant genes identified in previous work, the 56 variable genes were not located in subtelomeric regions.
source: Unlike clonally variant genes identified in previous work (Rovira-Graells et al., 2012), these 56 genes were not located in subtelomeric regions.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of the 56 variable genes.

claim: The products of the 56 variable genes were involved in nucleosome assembly, the proteasome and vacuolar acidification.
source: The products of these genes were involved in nucleosome assembly, the proteasome and vacuolar acidification, suggesting a role in controlling gene expression through transcription initiation, protein stability and protein localisation.
evidence: This is a result from the functional enrichment analysis.

claim: The 56 variable genes have moderately longer than average half lives.
source: From a published dataset of mRNA half-lives in the asexual cycle, we found that these genes actually have moderately longer than average half lives (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of mRNA half-lives shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The variability of the 56 genes was more likely to be driven by variable transcription initiation than by rapid decay.
source: This suggests that the variability of these genes was more likely to be driven by variable transcription initiation than by rapid decay.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the half-life analysis.

claim: The 56 variable genes are more conserved in evolution than expected by chance.
source: We found that these genes are more conserved in evolution than expected by chance (p=2.2e-16), and that that this is not simply because they tend to be highly expressed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a result from the conservation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 22 of the 56 variable genes in P. falciparum asexual stages are also variably expressed genes in the sexual stages.
source: Intriguingly, 22 of these 56 genes are also variably expressed genes in the sexual stages, suggesting an intrinsic variability across the life cycle (Supplementary file 3E).
evidence: This is a result from comparing variable genes across life stages.

claim: The most variably expressed genes in sexual stages were those from contingency gene families: var in P. falciparum and pir in P. berghei.
source: Surprisingly, the most variably expressed genes in sexual stages were those from contingency gene families: var in P. falciparum and pir in P. berghei (Figure 6; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of variable genes in sexual stages shown in Figure 6.

claim: In P. berghei male gametocytes, significant variability of a set of pir genes was observed.
source: In P. berghei male gametocytes, we observed significant variability of a set of pir genes (Otto et al., 2014) (p=0.014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 4), whose protein products have previously been identified in male gametes (Talman et al., 2014), indicating a potential role in fertilization.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of P. berghei male gametocytes shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Protein products of variably expressed pir genes have previously been identified in male gametes.
source: In P. berghei male gametocytes, we observed significant variability of a set of pir genes (Otto et al., 2014) (p=0.014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 4), whose protein products have previously been identified in male gametes (Talman et al., 2014), indicating a potential role in fertilization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Talman et al., 2014.

claim: P. berghei females showed transcriptional variation in members of subtelomeric multigene families fam-a and fam-b.
source: We found no female-specific pir genes, instead, females showed transcriptional variation in members of subtelomeric multigene families fam-a and fam-b (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of P. berghei female gametocytes shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Within any single P. falciparum female cell, only a single var gene had reads supporting correct splicing.
source: We found that within any single female cell, only a single var gene had reads supporting correct splicing, suggesting that mutually exclusive expression of var genes occurs in sexual stages, as it does in asexual parasites (Guizetti and Scherf, 2013).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of var gene expression in P. falciparum females.

claim: Mutually exclusive expression of var genes occurs in sexual stages, as it does in asexual parasites.
source: We found that within any single female cell, only a single var gene had reads supporting correct splicing, suggesting that mutually exclusive expression of var genes occurs in sexual stages, as it does in asexual parasites (Guizetti and Scherf, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the single var gene expression pattern, supported by a citation.

claim: The coding var transcripts in P. falciparum females were always from internal var gene clusters, often with the upsC class of promoters.
source: The coding var transcripts were always from internal var gene clusters, often with the upsC class of promoters, distinct from the subtelomeric var genes seen in asexual stages, with upsB and upsA promoters (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of var gene expression shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Male gametocytes only ever showed mRNA from a single var gene, var2csa.
source: Male gametocytes only ever showed mRNA from a single var gene, var2csa, known for its importance in pregnancy related malaria (Figure 6B; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of bulk male gametocyte RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: var2csa has been proposed as an important regulator of var gene expression switching.
source: This gene has also been proposed as an important regulator of var gene expression switching (Mok et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mok et al., 2008.

claim: Gametocytes show significant sex-specific variation in expression of large multigene families.
source: Our novel observation that gametocytes show significant sex-specific variation in expression of large multigene families, hitherto known for their importance in asexual stages, suggests that their evolution and function may also be driven by sexual stage biology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of multigene family expression in gametocytes.

claim: A marked, conserved sex-specific pattern of transcription factor expression was observed in both species.
source: We observed a marked, conserved sex-specific pattern of TF expression (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of transcription factor expression shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: One female-specific transcription factor (ap2-o) has been previously shown to have a female function and is likely to have a role in differentiating male and female forms.
source: Interestingly, one female-specific TF in particular (ap2-o) has been previously shown to have a female function and is likely to have a role in differentiating male and female forms (Modrzynska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Modrzynska et al., 2017.

claim: The optimised protocol enables evaluation of full length transcripts.
source: This protocol enables evaluation of full length transcripts, something required for evaluating the complex transcriptional patterns we observed for var genes but which is not currently possible with 3' tag-based approaches (Poran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the protocol.

source: We speculate that the sharp transitions we have observed correspond to such checkpoints.

source: Most genes are known to vary during the asexual, blood stage cell cycle with a single peak of expression (Bozdech et al., 2003a).

source: But unexpectedly we found another class of genes varying independently of the cell cycle both in cycling and arrested cells.

source: We found that, unlike contingency genes, they were highly conserved between species and the same types of genes were variable in parasite species infecting both humans and rodents.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of cell-cycle-independent variable genes.

claim: Generating variation in a population of many millions of closely related parasites occupying an ever varying host environment may be a bet-hedging strategy favouring success of at least some of the members of this population.
source: Generating variation in a population of many millions of closely related parasites occupying an ever varying host environment may be a bet-hedging strategy favouring success of at least some of the members of this population.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the biological significance of the variation.
